summary: Reports on an IAB workshop at the University of Cambridge in December 2013 on Internet technology adoption and transition. It examines economic models, especially at the waist of the hourglass in the protocol stack, with no single set of recommendations.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7305 reports on a workshop held by the Internet Architecture Board about why some new Internet protocols are adopted widely and others are not. Participants from network operations, research and engineering looked at the economics of adoption and at the obstacles each protocol faces. They agreed there is no single answer, but they identified incentives, bundling and workable deployment paths as the parts worth studying further.

questions: what factors make internet protocols successful
why has ipv6 adoption been slow
how does bundling affect protocol adoption
what role do incentives play in protocol deployment
subtitle: A report from an IAB workshop on why some Internet protocols spread and others stall.

tldr.problem: Good engineering is not enough to make a new Internet protocol widely used, because the cost of adopting it often falls on parties who gain nothing from it.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet Architecture Board held a two-day workshop in Cambridge in December 2013 and collected research on the economics of adoption, bundling, incentives, standards practice and the feasibility of protocols such as Multipath TCP and DNSSEC.
tldr.outcome: The report names no single fix. It lists the factors that were seen to matter, points to a research gap between researchers and standards bodies, and proposes follow-up work for the IAB, the IETF, the IRTF and registry organisations.

today: RFC 7305 is an Informational report published in July 2014, and the unit metadata lists no document that obsoletes or updates it. It records what the participants said at one workshop in 2013, so it is a snapshot of the thinking at that time rather than a specification anyone implements.

sections.title: Why the Workshop Was Held
sections.content:
The document records a workshop hosted by the University of Cambridge on December 4 and 5, 2013. The Internet Architecture Board runs such workshops to consider long-term questions about the Internet and to suggest future directions for its architecture, alongside the day-to-day engineering work of the IETF working groups.

The starting point is the shape of the Internet's protocol stack, described as an hourglass with IP in the middle: many protocols above it, such as HTTP and TCP, and many below it, such as Ethernet and the physical layer. Changing the narrow middle of that shape is hard. The report notes that most protocols have strong externalities, meaning one party's choice or cost affects other parties who had no say, and that a well-established incumbent makes this worse. Factors outside the control of the endpoints, such as middleboxes, can limit deployment, sometimes by design.

The workshop therefore asked two questions: what makes a protocol design successful and able to keep evolving, and what deployment strategies let a new feature gain enough ground to become widely used. Participants were operators, researchers in computer science and economics, and engineers. Because the contributions were wide ranging, the report makes few recommendations.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop asked a practical question: a protocol can be well designed and still never be used. The report explains that the Internet's protocol stack has a narrow middle, where changes are hardest, and that the people asked to change their equipment rarely get anything back for it.

sections.title: The Narrow Middle of the Protocol Stack
sections.content:
The workshop opened by asking whether the narrow middle of the hourglass is closed for business. Three cases of slow progress were named: IPv6, the Stream Control Transmission Protocol and DNS Security. DNSSEC was of particular interest because other services depend on it, including DANE, which authenticates named entities for TLS, and because application discovery through DNS could use it. A slow middle, the report observes, holds back the parts above it.

One suggestion was that the narrow point might in fact be as high as the application layer, with HTTP as the new neck. This was rebutted on the grounds that protocols do keep evolving: SMTP and IMAP in the application space have continued to change, as has the transport layer.

The group then reviewed RFC 5218, which lists protocol success factors and had been presented at the IETF 70 plenary. Two outcomes followed: the IAB should apply that document when it evaluates proposals for Birds of a Feather sessions, so that each proposed working group addresses a specific design space and can show positive net value; and the community should keep tracking works by their outcome, success, wild success or failure. Failure was described as the hardest of the four to judge, particularly in the narrow middle of the stack.
sections.plainLanguage: Three well-known protocols, IPv6, SCTP and DNSSEC, had been slow to spread, and the group looked at why. It also reviewed an earlier IETF document, RFC 5218, which lists what makes a protocol succeed, and agreed that the IAB should use that list when it decides which new working groups to allow.

sections.title: Bundling, Rewards and Incentives
sections.content:
Several papers looked at the economics of adoption. The first examined bundling, meaning shipping two technologies together. Bundling helps when one technology only becomes worth having once enough people use it, and a second technology with a low adoption cost and immediate value draws in the early users until the critical mass exists for the first. This matters to the IETF because of layering and the practice of marking a feature mandatory to implement. Current examples given were DANE on top of DNSSEC and WebRTC on top of SCTP. Whether bundling helps depends on the costs, benefits and externalities of each technology.

The second paper looked at Bitcoin, which overcame adverse press, legal uncertainty, glitches and breaches, previous failed attempts and speculative attacks. Three factors were credited: a built-in reward for early adopters, paid at an exponentially declining rate; the ability to exchange the currency directly for other currencies; and a store of value that people find in the currency itself. The first two may transfer to other protocols. The report draws out two protocol success factors from them, a direct benefit to the participant and the ability to interface with other systems for mutual benefit, noting that email succeeded partly through simpler adaptation to non-Internet email systems, and offering the plainest version of all, IP over everything. The key message is that if a protocol imposes costs on other systems, an incentive must be found for those parties to implement it.

The third paper reported on the .SE registry, which manages about 1.5 million domains under the Swedish country code top-level domain. .SE began by mapping its ecosystem and its stakeholders, then charged extra for DNSSEC, which did not work well. It funded the development of OpenDNSSEC to remove a technical barrier, though more tooling and an interface between the signing zone and the registrar were still needed. The Swedish government gave financial incentives to domain holders, and .SE gave incentives to registrars. The pattern was to examine every player and give each of them a reason to take part. The group noted that .SE could subsidise deployment because it could set its own prices, and that the margins of other registries did not allow the same reduction.
sections.plainLanguage: Three studies pointed the same way. Pairing a technology with one that people will adopt anyway can help it reach enough users to be worth having. Giving the early users a direct reward works, as Bitcoin showed. And when a new protocol costs other parties money, those parties need a reason to pay it, which is what the Swedish domain registry did for DNSSEC by rewarding registrars and domain owners.

sections.title: Judging Feasibility and Choosing Mechanisms
sections.content:
One paper offered an interactive approach to deciding whether IETF work is likely to be adopted, combining value net analysis, deployment environment analysis and technical architecture analysis, leading to feasibility and solution analysis. It overlapped with RFC 5218 in many points. The case study was Multipath TCP. Widening the bandwidth in the network seemed to reduce the attraction of Multipath TCP, the benefit against cost was not attractive to vendors, and the parties involved did not all agree on the benefits. The proposed ways to improve deployment included using open source software, lobbying implementers, deploying proxies, and completing implementations where one party owns both ends of a connection.

A recurring theme was to stop asking when a choice must be made between two technologies and instead implement several mechanisms, each of which can then drive adoption. The case discussed was Skype, which uses the best available transport rather than tying itself to one, and the report notes this as an adaptation of the Happy Eyeballs approach of RFC 6555. The paper also recorded a theme that is best effort service can be a deployment success factor in its own right.

Other sessions looked at the complexity of designed systems, comparing the hourglass with the bow tie model from systems biology, where adenosine triphosphate sits at the centre in the way IP does in the Internet, and at the idea of systems that are robust yet fragile, since highly efficient systems can prove fragile in the face of failure and hard to evolve. The answer to what engineers should take from systems biology was that more work is needed, with network management named as a promising area. A study of technology transitions in Japan at the link, IP and application layers found a phase difference in the diversity trend between each layer, that HTTP is the predominant substrate for other applications, and that natural selection is a strong force. A paper on economic models of network technology adoption looked at smart data pricing, in which time-dependent pricing let a provider shift traffic to off-peak periods, with Explicit Congestion Notification and RADIUS used alongside a simple graphical interface.
sections.plainLanguage: One group of papers asked how to tell, early on, whether a protocol will actually be deployed. Multipath TCP was the test case, and the answer was discouraging: more bandwidth made it less attractive, vendors did not see the cost as worth it, and the parties disagreed about the benefits. A second group suggested a practical tactic, which is to ship several ways of doing the same thing and let the best one win, as Skype does with its transports.

sections.title: Making Standards Better and Other Challenges
sections.content:
On how standards are produced, one paper treated patents as a barrier to deployment, in particular the unseen patent of the non-practising entity, but the discussion also looked at patents as a means to improve interoperability, since a patent holder who licenses in a particular way can push a single approach to standardisation. A second paper examined the gap between researchers and standards organisations, using mobile traffic offloading and IPv6 transition technologies as case studies. The offloading mechanism needed to be understood in both 3GPP and IETF terms, and met resistance in both: 3GPP already had an offloading model, and in the IETF there was a lack of understanding of the interdisciplinary space. The researchers thought they had taken the wrong approach by proposing a solution without first fully explaining the problem. On IPv6 transition they found a crowded field and little appetite for new work. The group asked whether the standards arena is the best measure of success for researchers, and noted that the IRTF is meant to bridge academic research and the IETF.

A third discussion asked whether the existing architecture serves the broadest set of needs, looking at geographic, technical and socioeconomic aspects. Researchers presented an alternative architecture, Lowest Common Denominator Networking, which re-examines base assumptions including the always-on nature of the Internet. The group questioned many of the baseline assumptions of the researchers, in part because the discussion time was short and a fuller explanation was warranted.

Two further topics were raised. On routing security, a presentation applied the tragedy of the commons to global inter-domain routing: the Internet Commons is a collection of networks that people depend on but do not control, and the main threat in BGP is routing pollution, unwanted or unnecessary routing entries. The Internet Society has worked with service providers to build a shared understanding of the problem and of risks and benefits, so that operators will cooperate reciprocally. What was notable in the discussion was that there is no magic bullet, and that the work is a matter of identifying the key players and showing them their incentives align, together with ways to measure resiliency. On TLS, the original plan to discuss whether the IETF could mandate stronger security turned into a discussion of reaching the next version of the protocol. Many old versions were still in existence because of old implementations, and a substantial amount of traffic was still encrypted with Triple DES. Concerns included that perfect could become the enemy of good, that a testing platform might help interoperability, and that the promotion of new versions of TLS is itself unresolved.
sections.plainLanguage: Three practical problems were debated. Patent holders can shape which version of a standard wins. Researchers who propose a fix without first explaining the problem run into resistance in standards bodies. And routing security has no technical single answer, because every operator benefits from a safer routing system while each also benefits from others paying for the protection, so the work is about showing operators that their incentives line up.

sections.title: Outcomes and Next Steps
sections.content:
The report is explicit that there is no single silver bullet for making a protocol successful, and it lists the follow-up items the participants agreed on. For the IAB and the IETF: apply the lessons of RFC 5218 when giving advice on Birds of a Feather sessions and working group charters; track and present protocol success stories, including first-mover advantages, for example through wikis or plenary discussions; and consider standardising the provisioning interface for DNSSEC keys between a parent zone and a child zone, where contributions would be welcome.

For the IRTF, two possible research groups were suggested. One would consider protocol alternatives and recommendations for constrained environments, limited by bandwidth or other resources, and such a group had already been proposed. The other would focus on the economic considerations of protocol design, with bundling and systems biology named as examples of areas that deserve investigation and collaboration between researchers, engineers and operators.

For others, the report notes that incentive models involve many players, so organisations such as ICANN and the Regional Internet Registries can keep encouraging deployment through their policies, with a specific role for the registries in routing security and for ICANN in securing the domain name service. A suggestion was made that IETF working groups draw on graduate students to help review Internet-Drafts and RFCs, which would give students an education in the real processes, engage the research community more thoroughly and add capacity to the review workload; several attendees with such students were prepared to try it.
sections.plainLanguage: The workshop closed with a list of possible next steps rather than a decision. The IAB could apply the existing success checklist when it approves new working groups and keep a record of which protocols succeed. The IRTF could start research groups on protocols for constrained networks and on the economics of protocol design. Registry organisations could keep using their pricing and policy tools to reward deployment.

viz.caption: FACTORS NAMED IN THE REPORT AS HELPING A PROTOCOL SPREAD

items.title: Direct benefit
items.text: Early participants gain something for themselves, as Bitcoin miners earn coins.

items.title: A way to exchange
items.text: A protocol can be converted to or from something people already hold.

items.title: Incentives for others
items.text: Parties who bear the cost of the change are given a reason to pay it.

items.title: Bundling
items.text: Two technologies ship together until one reaches critical mass.

items.title: Several mechanisms
items.text: Ship more than one way of doing the same thing and let the best one win.

items.title: Interoperability
items.text: The protocol reaches systems that already exist, as email did with non-Internet mail.
